units.title: 四级匹配：潮池观察活动的路线记录
units.instruction: Read the whole article. Match each statement to paragraph A–K. A paragraph may be used more than once or not at all.

materials.title: The Shore Did Not Keep the Same Path
materials.text:
This original fictional case supplies all evidence needed for the questions.

A

The Seaford nature club planned a short public walk among rock pools. Its old leaflet showed a winding path and promised that visitors would see several familiar sea creatures. When leader Dan reviewed the leaflet, he saw two different sorts of claim. The route described where a group could walk under certain conditions. The animals were possibilities, not appointments. He rewrote the introduction to explain the walk’s purpose: careful observation of a changing shore, rather than a guarantee that a particular list of living things would appear for inspection.

B

The meeting time was chosen from a local tide plan, with additional checks of the conditions relevant to the route. A clock time used for a previous outing could not simply be copied to the next date. Dan recorded the date and the source of the planning information. The leaflet told participants to follow the announced arrangements and the leader’s decisions on the day, not to treat the printed route as permission for an independent walk at any hour. A diagram described a planned activity; it did not hold the water level still.

C

The route had alternatives. One passage between rocks was narrow and uneven, while another offered a firmer approach to a smaller set of pools. Participants were told this before joining. Choosing the second route was not described as failing the activity. The purpose was observation, and the number of pools visited was not the only measure of a useful morning. Dan discussed needs with participants without assuming that age alone determined which route a person could use. A detailed description of the terrain was more useful than one broad label such as easy.

D

The club supplied a simple viewing tray for temporary observation under its stated procedure. An organism’s return location was noted when it was collected, so it could be put back where it had been found. The group did not treat all nearby pools as interchangeable homes. A tray made details easier to discuss, but it changed the context in which an animal was viewed. The guide distinguished observations made in the tray from those made before collection. Any collection limits and handling decisions remained with the responsible leader.

E

Visitors recorded whether an entry was a confident identification or a broader description. A small moving animal could remain a small crab if the features needed for a more exact name were not visible. The club did not reward the longest species list regardless of reliability. Drawings and notes about shape could still be useful. A local specialist later reviewed selected records, but that review was not presented as proof that every uncertain sighting had become exact. The original description remained linked to any later identification and the evidence behind it.

F

A smooth pool with few visible animals initially disappointed one family. Dan asked them to describe the surface, shade and water movement rather than copy a neighbour’s busy list. Absence of a sighting was not proof that the pool contained no life. Some organisms could be hidden, and the group watched only briefly. A short observation could establish what had been noticed under those conditions. It could not turn an unexamined crevice into a confirmed empty space or describe the pool’s contents at every time of day.

G

The club’s photographs included both close views and images showing the surrounding pool. A close photograph could help identify a feature but hide the conditions in which it had appeared. Members recorded which images had been cropped or adjusted for display. The newsletter did not use a dramatic enlargement to imply that the animal was large in ordinary scale. A ruler was included where appropriate to show size. The photograph remained evidence with a viewpoint and purpose, not a complete replacement for the location and observation notes.

H

Children were invited to compare two descriptions before hearing a name from the leader. One child noticed colour, another movement and a third the place where the animal sheltered. The order encouraged them to contribute what they had actually seen rather than repeat the first confident answer. Dan then connected the observations with relevant identification features. He did not withhold every explanation until the end of the walk. The activity separated first observation from later discussion while keeping both parts of learning available to the group.

I

The club recorded litter separately from wildlife sightings. A plastic fragment could affect the site, but it was not classified as a natural object merely because it appeared beside one. Any removal followed the group’s arranged procedure, and uncertain objects were left for the leader to assess. The record named what had been observed and what action had been taken. This prevented a later photograph of a clean pool from being read as evidence that no litter had been present at the beginning of the visit.

J

Changes to the route were announced during the walk and written into the leader’s record afterwards. A section that became unsuitable was not kept simply because it appeared on the leaflet. Participants could see that the altered route was a response to conditions rather than an unexplained mistake. The club kept the old plan labelled as a plan, beside the account of what actually happened. Future organisers could learn from the difference without assuming the revised route was now safe or appropriate under every future set of conditions.

K

After the outing, the club asked participants what had helped them observe and what information had been missing before arrival. The report counted completed visits but also described choices and limitations. A family that saw fewer named animals might still have gained a better way of looking. Dan’s final leaflet remained an invitation to a guided activity, with conditions and contacts clearly stated. It offered a route into the shore’s changing detail rather than a checklist whose failure to appear would make the whole walk a disappointment.

questions.prompt: A brief failure to see animals was not taken as evidence that a pool contained no life.
questions.explanation: F隐藏和短观察使无所见不等于全池无生命。E具体身份不确定不是不存在，其他段无该消极证据边界。

questions.prompt: A previous outing’s clock time was not reused without reference to the new date’s tidal conditions.
questions.explanation: B旧场次时间不能直接搬到新日期，按潮汐资料及现场条件安排，注明来源。J临场改路不同于预先日期选时；其他段无该时间依据。

questions.prompt: The plan and the actual route were retained as different records after conditions required a change.
questions.explanation: J临场不适改路，后记原计划与实际并存供学，非新路线永适。B预先潮汐安排不说明改后留两版；其他段无这项。

questions.prompt: Temporary observation outside a pool included a record of the organism’s original location.
questions.explanation: D观察盘暂取记返还地点，不把池都当一样，区分盘中与原位所见。G照片保地点不同于取出观察及归还；其他段无此安排。

questions.prompt: Participants first contributed their own observations before receiving an identification from the leader.
questions.explanation: H先比描述再听名字，免重复首个自信者，后接识别特征。E专家后来审记录非现场儿童发言顺序；其他段无此学习顺序。

questions.prompt: The leaflet did not authorise walking the printed route independently at any hour.
questions.explanation: B明确印图仅安排活动，须遵当天宣布和leader决定，不是任时自走许可。C可达路线描述不讲潮汐时段授权；其他段无此界线。

questions.prompt: A broad but supported description was preferred to an unjustifiably exact name.
questions.explanation: E可只记小蟹，辨别特征看不到不硬定种，专家复查亦有限。F未见不能证明空讨论负面观察非命名精度；其他段无此记录级别。

questions.prompt: A record of cleanup prevented a later tidy scene from concealing what had originally been found.
questions.explanation: I垃圾观察与行动分记，净池后照不能证明初无垃圾。G影像裁切说明不含清理前后区别；其他段无此行动改变现场的记录。

questions.prompt: A smaller, firmer route was treated as a valid way to participate rather than an unsuccessful version of the activity.
questions.explanation: C较少潮池的稳路非失败，先告地形不以年龄代具体需求。A观察目标总述不提供路线选择；其他段无此可达选项。

questions.prompt: Image selection included information needed to avoid misleading viewers about size and context.
questions.explanation: G近图加环境图，记裁调、适当尺度标，不以放大暗示实际大。D盘中改变情境但无照片尺度，其他段无这套影像记录。

units.instruction: Read the whole article. Match each statement to paragraph A–K. A paragraph may be used more than once or not at all.

materials.title: Before the Magazine Went to Print
materials.text:
This original fictional case supplies all evidence needed for the questions.

A

The Willow district magazine was produced by volunteers and delivered to local homes. Preparing an interview with a new theatre designer made its editors examine several habits they had never written down. A friendly conversation could become a published quotation, an attractive photograph could suggest a different story and a short deadline could leave no one sure who had checked a correction. The team made a small editorial guide. Its purpose was to clarify the work behind the pages, not to turn every volunteer into an expert in every possible publishing problem.

B

Interview notes distinguished exact recorded words from a reporter’s summary. Quotation marks were used only where the team could support the wording. A neat sentence written after the conversation might convey the reporter’s understanding without being something the interviewee had actually said. The editor could publish an attributed summary when appropriate, but it needed to look like a summary. The guide did not forbid editing an interview into a readable article. It required the form of presentation to match the kind of record the reporter had kept.

C

Before a conversation, the reporter explained the agreed uses of recording and quotation. A passage identified under their arrangement as background only remained outside the published quotations even if it would make an exciting headline. Permission to keep a private note for reporting was not automatically permission to publish it. Where a request changed after the interview, the editor checked the agreement and discussed the particular passage. The guide described this local process rather than assume that friendliness, possession of a recording or the absence of a later objection settled every question.

D

The designer’s photograph showed her beside an unfinished stage model. A suggested caption claimed that the model was the final design. The image alone could not establish that stage of work. Staff checked the caption with the project record and described it as a work in progress. A headline was reviewed for the same reason: a lively phrase should not turn an uncertain or qualified claim into a stronger one. The picture, caption and heading formed part of the published account, not decorations exempt from accuracy checks.

E

One local company paid for a page describing its new service. The magazine labelled the page as advertising and kept it distinct from the volunteer-written interview. The company could check facts about its own offering within the advertisement, but it did not gain control over unrelated editorial pages. The guide also rejected the idea that an unpaid page was automatically independent of every influence. The visible label identified a particular commercial relationship. It did not replace the editors’ responsibility to explain other relevant connections where those could affect a reader’s interpretation.

F

Letters to the editor could appear under a shortened name, but the team normally asked for a private way to contact the writer. This helped staff investigate questions before publication. The contact information did not appear in the printed letters column. An anonymous public signature and an uncontactable submission were therefore different situations. The guide explained the distinction to contributors instead of inviting people to assume that requesting a name privately meant every personal detail would be printed. Staff also checked factual allegations rather than publish them merely because someone had signed a letter.

G

A mistaken opening date in an earlier issue required more than changing a stored file. Readers of the printed magazine could not receive a silent update. The next issue carried a correction identifying the earlier error and the right date. The online copy linked to that notice while retaining an account of the change. The editors scaled the explanation to the error’s effect, not simply the number of letters replaced. One wrong date could alter a visitor’s plans even though correcting it occupied only a small amount of space.

H

The online edition showed how often articles were opened. Staff resisted treating this as an exact ranking of what every resident cared about. A story placed at the top of the page received more opportunities to be seen, and some residents used only the printed copy. The team considered requests and conversations alongside the digital totals. The data could inform future choices, but visibility and audience access had helped produce those totals. The guide named that limitation rather than discard the records or convert them into a complete portrait of local interest.

I

Digital pictures needed descriptions for readers who could not inspect the image. A useful description stated relevant visible features without pretending to know a subject’s inner thoughts. In the stage-model photograph, it could describe the designer’s position and the unfinished structure. It should not announce that she was satisfied with the final result. The editors checked these descriptions with the article’s purpose and facts. Accessibility text was another part of the publication’s account, subject to care and revision rather than a technical box to be filled after editing had ended.

J

The issue had a scheduled publication date, a time when the online version became visible and a delivery period for printed copies. These did not always coincide. A claim that every resident received an announcement on the issue date would therefore be unsupported. Staff recorded the stages separately when timing mattered, such as a public-event notice. The team could explain what it controlled and what depended on distribution. A date printed on the cover identified the issue; it did not prove the exact moment any individual reader encountered it.

K

After publication, the editors invited corrections and kept a list of unresolved questions for the next meeting. They did not promise to print every contribution or accept every proposed change. Instead, they explained the criteria and contact route. The guide remained short enough for volunteers to use, with examples from their own work. Its value was in making important distinctions available at the right moment: quote and summary, advertising and editorial choice, publication and delivery, private verification and public identification. Each helped readers understand what the magazine was actually claiming.

questions.prompt: Descriptions intended for image access were checked for unsupported claims about a person’s feelings.
questions.explanation: I辅助图文可写可见位置结构，不能写满意最终，需事实审。D caption核设计阶段无心理猜测或辅助访问具体规则；其他段无该要求。

questions.prompt: A photograph’s caption was checked because the picture did not establish whether a design was final.
questions.explanation: D未完模型照片不能证最终设计，核记录改work in progress，标题也受审。I图像辅助描述有关但未讲完成阶段核验；其他段无该caption事实。

questions.prompt: A background-only passage was handled according to the agreed interview use even when it could supply an attractive headline.
questions.explanation: C明确背景段再精彩也不入公开引语，变更须核约并讨论。D有标题核验但非背景授权条件；其他段无这项约定。

questions.prompt: A publicly shortened name was compatible with a private route for verifying a letter.
questions.explanation: F信栏缩名可仍私留联系方式，私核不全公示。C访谈背景约定非投书署名渠道；其他段无该匿名与可联络之别。

questions.prompt: The presentation of a statement reflected whether the notes supported exact words or only a summary.
questions.explanation: B记录原话与摘要分，只有可证措辞加引号，归属摘要不能装成逐字引语。D标题准确涉及强弱而非原话记录类型；其他段无该区分。

questions.prompt: The issue’s cover date did not demonstrate when every reader received its contents.
questions.explanation: J计划出刊、网络可见、纸配送不一，封面日期不证个人遇见时点。G旧刊更正是版本状态非传递时点；其他段无此阶段记录。

questions.prompt: A correction had to reach readers of a past printed issue rather than exist only as a silent digital edit.
questions.explanation: G印本不会被静默更新，下期更正旧误新日期，网链记录。J发行时间分stage不处理旧刊改错；其他段无此传播修订。

questions.prompt: Keeping a recording did not itself grant permission to publish every passage.
questions.explanation: C约定背景段不进引文，留私人笔记非发布许可，持录音不自解决。F私下联系信息不同于访谈引语授权；其他段无录音用途协议。

questions.prompt: Prominent online placement and use of print copies limited what opening counts could reveal about residents’ interests.
questions.explanation: H置顶曝光多、印本群体不在点击，不能全体偏好排行。E广告标签不包含这个计数选择机制；其他段无点击解释边界。

questions.prompt: A paid page was labelled without giving its purchaser authority over unrelated editorial material.
questions.explanation: E商业页标广告，公司核自身事实不控制采访等编辑页。H点击影响选题是读者数据不谈付款控制；其他段无此商业界线。

materials.title: The Joint That Fitted Yesterday
materials.text:
This original fictional case supplies all evidence needed for the questions.

A

A community woodwork group built small display stands for a local exhibition. One stand fitted neatly in the workshop but became difficult to assemble at the venue. Members first blamed the person who had packed it. Looking more closely, they found several possibilities: an altered environment, parts from different stands and a sequence that had not been written down. The group began documenting the design and assembly rather than treat a successful first build as a guarantee that every later user could reproduce it from appearance alone.

B

Pieces were labelled with the stand they belonged to and their place within it. Two rails could have similar lengths but slightly different end details. They were not treated as interchangeable merely because they looked alike in a box. The group kept a parts list and checked it before transport. When a replacement was made, its identifier was linked to the stand’s record. This made it possible to distinguish an original component, a substituted one and an item packed accidentally from a neighbouring project.

C

The drawing stated dimensions and units together. A number without a unit could be read differently by someone using another ruler or another part of the plan. Members also marked which measurements referred to an opening and which to the piece intended to fit into it. Equal written numbers did not always mean the pieces should be cut to exactly equal dimensions. The group discussed the required relationship with its instructor rather than assume that copying a numeral alone completed the task of interpreting a design.

D

A trial assembly was made before final finishing. Members checked whether parts met in the intended order and whether tools could reach the relevant points. Applying a surface finish first could hide a problem until changing the fit became more awkward. The trial was labelled as a check under workshop conditions. It did not justify promising that no adjustment would be needed after transport. The group recorded what had been tried, including the actual components used, so later assembly would not depend on a memory that it had worked once.

E

Wood could respond to environmental conditions. The instructor explained that a fit checked in one setting should be assessed again after a significant change in the surroundings. The group did not use this explanation to excuse every mismatch. A wrong part or a mistaken measurement still needed investigation. It separated possible material movement from errors in the plan or assembly. The venue record included relevant conditions without claiming that one observation had established how every species of wood would behave in every room.

F

The visible grain direction was noted where it mattered to the design. A decorative board chosen only for its colour might behave differently from another board placed in a different orientation. The instructor connected the markings on the drawing with the actual material before members began their supervised work. The discussion did not turn grain into an explanation for every fault. It gave the group a specific feature to inspect instead of assuming that all wooden pieces of the same outline were physically identical apart from their appearance.

G

The assembly guide named a sequence. One crosspiece had to be placed before a surrounding frame was closed; inserting it afterwards would require undoing earlier work. A finished photograph showed the result but not this dependency. The group added staged pictures and short instructions, each linked to a parts identifier. The guide did not attempt to replace appropriate instruction in unfamiliar tool use. Its purpose was to make the order of this particular build visible to members already working within the workshop’s supervised arrangements.

H

The exhibition would place objects on the stands. Members recorded the intended use and the checks agreed with their instructor instead of calling a stand suitable for any load. A small decorative sample did not establish unlimited strength. Organisers were asked to consult the group before changing what would be displayed. The label described a defined purpose rather than invite visitors to test the structure by leaning on it. Changing a load or arrangement was a change to the task the group had prepared, not merely a new artistic choice.

I

Surface treatment altered the appearance of sample boards. Under the workshop lamp, one finish looked closest to the organiser’s reference; under the venue lighting, another looked different again. The group kept labelled samples and considered them in the intended space. It did not promise that a photograph on every phone would show the same colour. The reference was used to discuss choices, while lighting and display conditions were recorded as part of the comparison. A similar image was not the only possible evidence of a suitable finish.

J

When a component was repaired, the record stated what was removed, added or altered. The group retained a photograph of the earlier condition and named the repair date. A later member could then tell why a piece no longer matched the first drawing exactly. The repaired stand was checked for its intended use again rather than assumed satisfactory because it had once passed a trial. Documentation was not intended to make a repair look dramatic. It helped separate the history of the object from the current conditions under which it could be used.

K

The final packing plan placed matching parts together and protected labelled surfaces from rubbing. Members timed disassembly and setup, discovering that the public exhibition occupied only part of the project’s work. A new volunteer tried the guide while an experienced member observed and noted unclear passages. The guide became more useful after this trial than after another person merely proofread its spelling. The group had learned to test not only whether a stand could be assembled, but whether its account of assembly could travel to someone who had not watched the original build.

questions.prompt: The object’s documented purpose did not authorise arbitrary changes to what it would support.
questions.explanation: H按约定展物及检查，不能任意荷载或靠压，改用途先咨询。D试装非承载用途，其他段无这个使用范围。

questions.prompt: The plans distinguished an opening’s dimensions from those of the part meant to fit into it.
questions.explanation: C数值需单位，还分开口与插入件，不能只复制同数切同。D试装查结果未先定义尺寸对象；其他段无这个量测关系。

questions.prompt: A changed component was explained through a repair history rather than silently judged against the first drawing.
questions.explanation: J记移增改、前照日期，解释与初图差，重核用途。B替换标识关联但不含修理前后变化记录；其他段无该修史。

questions.prompt: A change in surroundings could affect fit, but it did not rule out wrong parts or measurement errors.
questions.explanation: E木材环境响应是可能因素，仍查错件误量，非万能借口。F纹理方向属于材料具体特征而非环境前后；其他段无该排查边界。

questions.prompt: A new user tried the assembly instructions so unclear steps could be found through use.
questions.explanation: K新志愿者按指南、老成员看，实测比仅校字更显不懂处。G写分阶段说明非新用户试读行为；其他段无这个可用性核验。

questions.prompt: A finished image did not reveal that one component had to be inserted before another stage was closed.
questions.explanation: G横件先于闭框，成品照不示依赖，加分阶段图及标号。K新手试指南不说明这条结构先后；其他段无该具体序列。

questions.prompt: Similar-looking components were identified so parts from different stands would not be confused.
questions.explanation: B按架号及位置标rail、列清单、替换关联，外观近非互换。C测量单位是设计解释非实物归属；其他段无该标识系统。

questions.prompt: Finish samples were compared in the intended venue because lighting could change their appearance.
questions.explanation: I带标签样板到场比较，车间灯与现场不同，不保证手机色同。E环境影响尺寸不是光照外观；其他段无饰面照明比较。

questions.prompt: Assembly was checked before finishing because later surface work could make correction more awkward.
questions.explanation: D先试拼再表面处理，防后隐问题更难改，记实际部件。I饰面颜色对比非装配先后；其他段无这项阶段选择。

questions.prompt: Material orientation was recorded rather than treating every wooden outline as physically equivalent.
questions.explanation: F记木纹方向并连实际料，不能外形同就物理一样。B同长异端是零件身份而非纹理取向；其他段无此。

units.instruction: Read the whole article. Match each statement to paragraph A–K. A paragraph may be used more than once or not at all.

materials.title: The Weight Written on the Sack
materials.text:
This original fictional case supplies all evidence needed for the questions.

A

A small farming cooperative shared a grain store after harvest. Members expected a larger building to solve the confusion of keeping sacks in several barns. The new store offered more space, but its first week showed that space alone did not explain whose grain was where or which figure should appear on a receipt. The cooperative introduced a record connecting arrival, weighing, storage and collection. It aimed to make a shared service understandable to its members, rather than let the person who happened to be on duty become the only source of knowledge.

B

The weighing form separated the mass of a filled container from the mass of the grain inside it. The empty container contributed to the total, and different sacks or boxes did not necessarily weigh the same. Staff recorded the relevant empty-container allowance instead of calling every displayed scale number the grain’s own weight. A full box could show a larger total than a sack while holding less grain. The form named the quantities so members could compare the content rather than unknowingly compare the content together with unlike packaging.

C

Before weighing deliveries, staff checked the scale’s starting indication and followed the cooperative’s agreed verification routine. A display that returned to zero was useful information but did not by itself establish accuracy over every possible load. The store kept the verification record and the date of any service. If an unusual reading appeared, the staff did not assume either that the farmer had supplied a wrong amount or that the scale must be broken. They checked the relevant conditions and records before deciding what the discrepancy might mean.

D

The cooperative’s stated agreement distinguished received weight from the quantity used for payment under its moisture policy. A wetter batch could carry more water, so comparing raw delivered totals alone would not answer every commercial question. The policy and the measurement used were explained before members delivered grain. The store did not present its local agreement as a rule that every market followed. A receipt needed to make clear whether a number described what arrived or a calculation under the agreed basis, so two different quantities would not be mistaken for contradictory measurements.

E

A small sample was not allowed to speak for an entire delivery without a described sampling method. Grain could vary across bags or within a load. Staff recorded where samples had come from and what assessment they supported. A clean handful taken from the easiest place was not automatically representative of every sack. The cooperative used the assessment within the scope of its procedure and recorded unresolved questions. The record distinguished an examined portion from the whole delivery, even where a shared classification was later applied under the agreement.

F

Every lot received an identifier linked to its contributor and arrival record. Reused sacks could still carry an earlier owner’s name, so the writing already printed on a bag was not treated as the authoritative identity of its current contents. Staff attached the new identifier in a way that remained visible after stacking. A member collecting grain could then refer to the lot record rather than search only for a familiar-looking sack. The system separated a useful physical container from the historical and ownership information assigned to the grain inside it.

G

The store map showed where each lot had been placed. When sacks moved to make room, the transaction was recorded rather than left for the next shift to remember. A map with yesterday’s locations could look precise while sending someone to the wrong stack. The cooperative linked the location record with the movement date and the responsible staff member. The map remained a guide to current storage, not a decorative floor plan. Updating it was part of moving grain, rather than an optional office task to be completed when the store became quiet.

H

A torn sack was set apart for inspection and its contents protected under the store’s procedure. This did not mean the grain had automatically been condemned or transferred to another member. The record described the damaged packaging and the action taken. Staff distinguished a problem with a container from a conclusion about the quality or ownership of everything inside it. If a new sack was needed, the lot identifier travelled with the contents. Otherwise, a repair could solve a physical problem while creating a new uncertainty about whose grain had been moved.

I

One entry used a count of sacks where a weight field required kilograms. Both numbers were real descriptions of something, but they were not interchangeable. The team corrected the record with an explanation and kept the original value visible in the change history. It then clarified the field label and checked nearby entries made in the same way. The lesson was not that every large or small number was suspicious. A value had to be interpreted with its unit and the thing counted or measured before it could be used in a total.

J

Collection involved a receipt identifying the lot, quantity and person receiving it. Staff recorded the handover time and obtained the confirmation required by the cooperative. That confirmation showed a documented transfer; it was not a new laboratory guarantee of grain quality. If the recipient raised a concern, it was noted rather than erased by the signature. The cooperative wanted the handover record to explain what had changed hands and under what stated conditions, not to give one mark on paper the power to settle every possible later question.

K

At the monthly meeting, members saw aggregate totals for storage and transactions alongside an account of unresolved discrepancies. Personal contact details and individual records were available only through the cooperative’s agreed access process. A public summary could show how the service was working without publishing every member’s information. The report did not hide uncertainty in order to make the new store appear perfect. It showed where the record was complete, where a check remained open and which procedure would be used to resolve it, making shared administration something members could inspect.

questions.prompt: A signed handover confirmed a transfer without becoming a new guarantee of product quality.
questions.explanation: J交接注明批量人时，确认只证转交非新质检，有异议仍记。D付款政策不是签收效力；其他段无此。

questions.prompt: The source and purpose of samples were recorded so an easy handful was not assumed to represent the whole delivery.
questions.explanation: E取样位置方法及支持评估有限，易取一把不自动代表全车。H破袋检查不是代表性抽样设计；其他段无此。

questions.prompt: Packaging weight was distinguished from the weight of the material being stored.
questions.explanation: B分满容器总重与粮重，空袋箱重量不同须扣记。D湿度合同计价是粮内水分而非外包装重量；其他段无该容器与内容区分。

questions.prompt: A damaged package was not automatically treated as proof that its contents were poor quality or had changed owners.
questions.explanation: H破袋另检保护、换袋带批号，容器问题不等粮质或产权结论。E抽样质量不讲袋破与归属，其他段无该边界。

questions.prompt: The receipt distinguished a received quantity from a figure calculated under a stated moisture agreement.
questions.explanation: D当地湿度政策分实收与计价量，事前解释，不泛称所有市场。B包装扣重无湿度支付依据；其他段无此合同量。

questions.prompt: Public reporting combined service totals with a limited route for accessing personal records.
questions.explanation: K月会汇总并报待查差异，个人联系和细账按约定访问不全公开。F批号追身份不是公示隐私范围；其他段无这个统计与访问分层。

questions.prompt: Moving stored material included updating a dated location record.
questions.explanation: G移袋腾地即记事务、位置日期责任人，昨日精图可能错。J取走交接记录不等于库内位置更新；其他段无当前库位图。

questions.prompt: A zero starting display was not treated as proof of accuracy across every load.
questions.explanation: C归零只是信息，还按验证例程留记录，不能全量程保证。I单位错是录入语义，不是秤校验范围；其他段无这条仪器界限。

questions.prompt: A count and a mass were recognised as different kinds of quantity despite both being genuine numbers.
questions.explanation: I袋数填公斤栏，数本身可真但单位对象不同，改留史并查邻项。C秤读数验证非计数质量单位区别；其他段无此错误。

questions.prompt: Existing writing on a reused container was not accepted as the current contents’ identity.
questions.explanation: F旧袋印名可旧主，当前批号绑贡献者到货，不能只认袋。B包装重不是身份，其他段无旧标与现物归属。

units.title: 六级匹配：试验指标与患者相关结果
units.instruction: Read the whole article. Match each statement to paragraph A–O. A paragraph may be used more than once or not at all.

materials.title: What Did the Trial Improve?
materials.text:
This original fictional case supplies all evidence needed for the questions.

A

A fictional trial evaluated a mobility-support programme. Its first announcement highlighted an improved movement score measured by a device. The research question, however, concerned whether people could function better in daily life. The score might contribute evidence without answering that whole question. The trial team prepared a fuller account explaining outcomes, procedures and uncertainty. It did not turn an encouraging measurement into a recommendation for every patient. The report asked readers to follow the connection between what the programme was intended to achieve and what the study had actually measured.

B

Before examining results, the team had identified a primary outcome and additional secondary outcomes. This order helped make the main question visible when several measures moved in different directions. A secondary result was not automatically unimportant, but it should not silently replace the primary measure simply because it looked more favourable. The report named each measure’s planned role. Where the analysis changed, the change was documented rather than described as though the revised question had been the sole purpose from the beginning of the trial.

C

The device score was considered a possible surrogate: a measurement standing in for an outcome people ultimately cared about. Association with daily functioning could make it informative, but did not guarantee that improving the score would improve that functioning. The programme might change one measured pathway without affecting all the processes that mattered. The team distinguished evidence that the score responded from evidence that patients benefited in the intended way. Calling the score a surrogate did not validate the substitution; the relationship itself required evidence.

D

Random assignment concerned the groups participants were offered, not a promise that everyone followed the assigned programme. Some attended fewer sessions and others stopped. Comparing people as assigned answered a question different from comparing only those who completed every activity. Completion could be related to health, circumstances or response. The team reported the analysis choices and what each was intended to estimate. It did not remove noncompleters without explanation and then treat the remaining comparison as automatically preserving all the protections of the original assignment.

E

Knowledge of the assigned programme could affect expectations and reporting. Where possible, staff assessing certain outcomes were kept unaware of allocation. Participants could not necessarily be unaware of an activity they had attended. The report described which parts were masked and which were not, instead of applying a single blinded label to the whole trial. This allowed readers to consider how knowledge might influence different measures. It did not imply that an unmasked observation was worthless or that masking removed every possible source of bias.

F

Some follow-up observations were missing. The team listed the amounts and reasons by group where known, rather than treat every missing entry as a successful outcome or a zero score. A person unavailable because of worsening health might differ from one who moved away for an unrelated reason. The available information could not identify every reason. Analyses therefore stated how they handled missing outcomes and examined reasonable alternatives. A high overall follow-up percentage did not remove the need to ask whether the remaining absence was related to the outcome.

G

The report used absolute and relative descriptions together. A hypothetical event rate changing from ten people in a hundred to eight represented a reduction of two percentage points and a relative reduction of one fifth. Neither description was inherently false, but they could produce different impressions if presented alone. The time period and the type of event were stated with the figures. A percentage without its denominator and reference could make a modest absolute change sound very large or prevent readers from understanding a potentially useful effect.

H

Possible harms were reported alongside benefits. The team did not combine them into one unexplained net-success number, because different people might give different weight to the outcomes. It recorded severity, frequency and observation period where the study could support them. The absence of a particular harm in a limited sample was not a guarantee that it could never occur. The report made room for a decision about trade-offs without pretending that the measurement alone selected one preference for every person who might later consider the programme.

I

Subgroup analyses examined whether patterns differed among participants. Some had been planned; others were suggested after the data were seen. The report labelled that distinction. A striking finding from many exploratory comparisons needed cautious interpretation and further evidence. Conversely, failure to demonstrate a difference in a small subgroup did not automatically prove no difference existed there. The team described estimates and uncertainty rather than use the words significant and nonsignificant as if they divided people into two permanently different biological categories.

J

A composite outcome joined several events into one measure. This could summarise part of the trial, but its interpretation depended on the components. A frequent mild event might drive the total even if a less common serious event did not change. The team reported components separately so readers could see what had produced the combined result. Sharing a place in the same statistic did not make all events equally important. The composite’s name had to be read with its definition rather than treated as a self-explanatory account of benefit.

K

The observation period was shorter than the time for which the programme might eventually be used. The team could describe what happened during follow-up, not certify the same effect indefinitely. A later loss of benefit or a delayed harm remained questions for further observation. The report did not dismiss the short-term evidence; it named its time boundary. A useful immediate change and an established long-term effect were different claims, even if a headline could express both with the same broad verb, improves.

L

Participants met stated eligibility rules. Some people with complex needs were not included, and the trial setting offered support that might differ elsewhere. The report described this population and context rather than imply that random assignment made the sample representative of every potential user. Internal comparison and external applicability answered different questions. A well-conducted estimate for those enrolled could be valuable while leaving uncertainty about people outside the study or about services unable to reproduce the conditions under which the programme had been delivered.

M

Participants also reported their sense of independence and ease of daily activity. These accounts were not discarded merely because they came from people rather than a device. Their interpretation still required attention to question wording, expectations and missing responses. The report kept them distinct from the movement score while recognising that they addressed experiences relevant to the trial’s aim. Objectively recorded and patient-reported did not form a simple ranking in which one category was always the only legitimate evidence and the other could never matter.

N

The public materials linked the protocol, analysis plan and subsequent amendments. Readers could see when a decision changed and what reason the team gave. An amendment was not automatically evidence of wrongdoing; an unexplained change could nevertheless make a result harder to interpret. The team preserved the sequence rather than overwrite every earlier plan with the final account. The documentation gave reviewers a way to distinguish a justified procedural revision from a result-dependent shift in the question, without having to infer the entire history from a polished final paper.

O

The final summary reported the movement-score result with the other outcomes and their limits. It avoided declaring either complete success or complete failure from one measure. The study contributed evidence within a population, period and set of procedures. Further decisions would involve that evidence and the values of people affected. The report’s task was to make the chain of reasoning inspectable, so a useful finding could be recognised without carrying claims about every outcome, person and future setting that the study had not examined.

questions.prompt: Missing follow-up was described by group and handled under stated assumptions rather than automatically coded as success.
questions.explanation: F列各组缺失原因，不能当成功或零，说明处理与替代假设。D未完成活动不等于随访缺数据；其他段无该空值方案。

questions.prompt: Earlier plans remained accessible so later procedural changes could be examined in sequence.
questions.explanation: N链接协议分析及修订，记时因不覆盖旧版，便辨合理修订和结果导向移题。B要求记主次变化未说明公开版本序列；其他段无此文档结构。

questions.prompt: A favourable additional measure was not allowed to silently replace the predeclared main question.
questions.explanation: B主次结果先定，次要非无用但不能因更好看暗换主，改动应记。N计划版本可核变化但不 specifically主次替换原则；其他段无此角色定义。

questions.prompt: Random allocation did not make the enrolled population representative of every possible user.
questions.explanation: L入选限制和试验支持环境异，内部随机比较不等外部代表。D随机遵从不同于人群外推；其他段无这个代表性区别。

questions.prompt: Improving a measurement used as a stand-in did not automatically establish improvement in the outcome it represented.
questions.explanation: C替代指标相关不保干预改分就改患者真实功能，路径可能不全。A是研究目标引入，J复合终点组分问题不同；其他段无替代验证论证。

questions.prompt: Participants’ own accounts were treated as relevant evidence while their production and limitations were examined.
questions.explanation: M独立和日常体验不因非设备丢弃，但看题措辞预期缺答，不搞客观对自报简单等级。E遮盲对报告影响不同于自报的价值地位；其他段无此论证。

questions.prompt: Two numerical descriptions of the same reduction were reported with their reference quantities.
questions.explanation: G十到八/百即两百分点与相对五分一，同事不同呈现，报期间事件。I亚组显著性不是绝对相对表达；其他段无这两算式。

questions.prompt: The report kept adverse outcomes visible instead of hiding different trade-offs inside an unexplained net result.
questions.explanation: H伤益并列记严重频率期间，不一数暗合权重，也无零伤保证。J复合事件解释非伤益价值取舍；其他段无这项呈报。

questions.prompt: The combined outcome was unpacked because frequent mild events could dominate its total.
questions.explanation: J复合指标需分组件，常见轻事可驱总量而严重事不变。H伤益分报不是同复合内事件贡献；其他段无此聚合机制。

questions.prompt: Restricting comparison to completers could change the question and lose benefits of the original allocation.
questions.explanation: D随机分配非保证遵从，完成者可能有健康条件筛选，不能不解释排未完者再当原随机。F随访缺失不同于仅完成者分析；其他段无此。

units.title: 六级匹配：数据迁移中需要保留的含义
units.instruction: Read the whole article. Match each statement to paragraph A–O. A paragraph may be used more than once or not at all.

materials.title: The Records Arrived, but Did They Mean the Same?
materials.text:
This original fictional case supplies all evidence needed for the questions.

A

A fictional booking service moved its records to a new database. The first report announced that every file had arrived and the number of rows matched. Users nevertheless saw some appointments at unexpected times. The migration team recognised that copying data and preserving its meaning were related but different tasks. A complete transfer could reproduce every character while the new application interpreted a field differently. The team revised its checks to follow the relationship between an old record, its intended interpretation and the behaviour that a user would encounter after the change.

B

Existing identifiers were kept or connected through an explicit mapping. A customer’s position in an exported list was not used as a substitute identity, because the list could be sorted differently on another run. The map also recorded relationships between bookings and customers. A new numeric value could be acceptable if the association was stable and documented, but silently assigning numbers by arrival order would make later comparison difficult. Identity belonged to a record’s history and links, not merely to the row in which it happened to appear during one export.

C

Some old times had been stored without a zone label, under an application convention known to the original team. The new system expected an explicit time interpretation. Appending a zone without checking that convention could shift an appointment while leaving its digits superficially familiar. The team documented the old assumption and converted relevant values accordingly. It distinguished the time of an event from the time a record was last updated. Both could look like timestamps, but they did not answer the same question and should not be substituted for each other.

D

Money fields had a similar problem. One system recorded a small monetary unit while another expected the major unit, and rounded display values did not always contain the precision of the stored amount. The migration specified units and conversion rules together. A value that passed a numeric type check could still be wrong by a large factor. The team compared representative transactions in their original units before approving the new interpretation, rather than assume that equal-looking columns implied identical financial quantities.

E

The old application distinguished an unanswered field, an empty string entered deliberately and a recorded zero. The new design initially grouped these together as blank. That simplified the interface but changed questions the data could answer. Zero participants was not the same as an unknown count, and a user clearing optional text could have a different meaning from a field never supplied. The team retained the required distinctions in its mapping and documented any information that the new model could not preserve, instead of silently presenting several states as one.

F

Category codes were mapped by their definitions rather than by their order in a list. An unfamiliar code was not automatically converted into the most common option. It was flagged for review under a stated procedure. The team also kept the source value so a later decision could be traced. This prevented a neat-looking destination table from hiding records whose meaning had never been established. Completeness did not require pretending that every source value had an obvious equivalent in the new vocabulary.

G

Related changes were handled as coherent units where the service required it. Moving a booking without its required relationship could create a record that existed but could not be interpreted correctly. The team checked links and the conditions under which a group of changes should succeed together or be left unapplied. It did not treat the absence of an individual row error as proof that the whole relationship was valid. A transaction-level check concerned how records fit together, not only whether each one satisfied a local field format.

H

Totals remained useful but were not treated as complete proof. Two incorrect records could offset one another in a sum, and duplicate rows could make a count look right while another item was absent. The team used counts, grouped quantities and selected record-level comparisons for different purposes. A matching checksum could establish that a file’s bytes were unchanged, not that the new software assigned the same meaning to them. Each check named the kind of failure it could detect rather than inherit authority from the general word verified.

I

A rehearsal used copies of representative data under controlled access. The sample included unusual statuses and relationships, not just recent ordinary records. Passing it could reveal important problems but did not certify every unexamined historical case. The team recorded the coverage of the rehearsal and expanded checks when a new class of issue appeared. It resisted two extremes: declaring all testing pointless because the sample was incomplete, or calling the whole migration proven because the most convenient examples had worked on the first attempt.

J

The process could stop and resume. To prevent a resumed run from creating a second copy of work already completed, operations had stable keys and a documented replay policy. A checkpoint recorded what had been accepted, not merely which line the script had last printed. The team tested an interruption followed by a restart. A successful uninterrupted run did not establish that this recovery path worked. Repetition needed to preserve the intended state rather than accumulate new bookings every time an operator tried again.

K

Users continued to make bookings while preparation was under way. The cutover plan identified which changes occurred after the initial copy and how they would reach the destination. It did not assume that a snapshot described a service that had stood still until launch. Reconciliation compared the relevant period and handled conflicts through stated rules. The team also checked the moment at which each source of writes changed responsibility. A plan for the first bulk transfer was incomplete without an account of the live changes around it.

L

Rollback required more than retaining an old database file. New records created after launch might need to be preserved, and the old software might not understand fields introduced by the new system. The team defined what could be reversed and how later changes would be handled before relying on a return path. A backup was necessary evidence of recoverability for some failures, not a universal guarantee that service could return unchanged at any time. The plan named both the protected information and the limits of the reversal.

M

Temporary copies could contain personal information. The migration used the organisation’s access and retention arrangements and avoided placing unnecessary sensitive fields in general debugging output. A technically convenient copy was not automatically appropriate for every colleague or external tool. Logs identified enough information to investigate a case without assuming more disclosure was always better. The team distinguished observability from unrestricted visibility. Documenting a failure could preserve accountability while still limiting which people and systems received the underlying records.

N

Historical migration scripts were retained with their original role in the system’s history. When a new correction was needed, the team added a forward change rather than rewriting the past script and pretending it had always performed the new operation. This made environments and records easier to compare. The history did not prove every old decision was ideal. It preserved the sequence of decisions so another operator could understand which transformations had actually occurred, especially when a current problem depended on how an earlier version had represented a field.

O

The final review included examples of appointments, amounts and relationships as users would encounter them. Specialists checked the documented meaning, while technical checks examined formats, links and execution. Neither role replaced the other. The service could then explain why it believed the migration preserved the relevant behaviour and which concerns remained open. The records had not merely arrived in a new location. They had crossed an interpretation boundary whose assumptions needed to be visible if users were to keep relying on the information as their own.

questions.prompt: Related records were checked as a coherent group rather than only as individually well-formed rows.
questions.explanation: G预约与必要关系需一起有效，组内全成或不成，格式合法不证关系。B身份映射不同于事务级一致；其他段无此检查范围。

questions.prompt: Digits resembling the old timestamp could still shift an event if the previous time convention was ignored.
questions.explanation: C旧无时区有应用约定，新显式时区须查解释，不然外观熟悉而预约偏移。K切换期间写入不是时区语义；其他段无该时间转译。

questions.prompt: Returning to the old system required a plan for post-launch records and new fields, not just an old backup.
questions.explanation: L旧库备份不能保证新写不失或旧程序识新字段，需先定逆转范围。K处理初拷后并发为上线计划，不 specifically退回旧版本兼容；其他段无该rollback边界。

questions.prompt: A recorded zero was preserved as distinct from an unanswered or deliberately cleared field.
questions.explanation: E旧系统区分未答、空串、零，不能新界面blank一并吞掉。D金额单位是数字含义另一例但非缺失状态；其他段无三态映射。

questions.prompt: The plan accounted for live changes made after the first copied snapshot.
questions.explanation: K初拷后仍用户写，需切换责任时点、增量达新端及冲突核对，不能想服务静止。J脚本重放不是用户并发新写；其他段无该切换窗口。

questions.prompt: Recovery was tested by interruption and replay because a clean continuous run did not prove safe resumption.
questions.explanation: J稳定键重放、验中断重启，检查点是真接受状态，不靠日志行，不得重复生预约。I样本覆盖未讲恢复路径；其他段无重放方案。

questions.prompt: A correction was added forward without rewriting a historical transformation as if it had always behaved differently.
questions.explanation: N保历史迁移，加前向纠正而不改旧脚本伪装旧操作，便追环境序列。L回滚限度不是改历史脚本政策；其他段无此。

questions.prompt: Stable identity was not replaced by a record’s position in a possibly reordered export.
questions.explanation: B列表排序可变不能按行位置当身份，保ID或显式映射及关联。J重跑稳定键相关但不 specifically导出位置身份；其他段无此顺序陷阱。

questions.prompt: Numeric conversion specified the monetary unit so a valid number would not become a greatly distorted amount.
questions.explanation: D小币单位与主单位、显示舍精度，按原单位比较，数类型正确不证钱数。E零未知区分不是币种量纲转换；其他段无货币单位。

questions.prompt: Matching totals or file digests did not alone establish that records were complete and interpreted correctly.
questions.explanation: H抵消错误、重行补漏、hash只字节，需分层核而不把verified全权。G跨记录事务是关系一致性，不讨论总量与字节界限；其他段无这些例。

units.title: 六级匹配：夜市摄影展中的同意与叙述
units.instruction: Read the whole article. Match each statement to paragraph A–O. A paragraph may be used more than once or not at all.

materials.title: The People Beyond the Frame
materials.text:
This original fictional case supplies all evidence needed for the questions.

A

A fictional neighbourhood project photographed a night market for an exhibition. The square was open to the public, and the photographers initially assumed that public visibility made every later use straightforward. Conversations with stallholders revealed a more complex set of responsibilities. The exhibition would select moments, attach descriptions and reach people who had never visited the market. The team began documenting these choices rather than treat the camera as a device that simply transferred a shared reality into a gallery without changing its audience or meaning.

B

The project’s consent process distinguished taking a photograph from displaying it in specified settings. A person might agree to a local wall exhibition without agreeing to an unrestricted promotional campaign. The team described proposed uses in understandable terms and kept a record of those permissions. It did not present its arrangement as a universal legal rule for all public photography. It was a responsibility the collaborators had explicitly adopted for this project, and possession of the file did not silently expand the uses to which the person had agreed.

C

A market organiser helped arrange introductions but could not automatically speak for every stallholder or visitor. The project separated logistical approval from individual participation under its consent plan. A shop association’s support did not make every member’s preference identical. Where a group portrait was proposed, the team considered the people actually involved rather than rely only on one representative’s enthusiasm. Coordination was valuable, but it was not treated as an unrestricted transfer of authority over all the people who happened to share a place or occupation.

D

Captions were checked for the difference between visible detail and inference. A photograph could show a person standing beside a stall, but it did not by itself establish income, ownership or emotional state. One draft described a seller as delighted with the night’s trade. The team replaced it with a supported account of the event after finding no basis for the claim about sales or feeling. A caption was an assertion made by the exhibition, not a neutral label protected from scrutiny merely because it sat beneath a real photograph.

E

Some short statements were translated for the display. The project kept the original wording and identified when the English text was a direct rendering or a summary. A fluent, polished sentence could otherwise look as though the speaker had chosen every word and emphasis in the display language. Contributors reviewed relevant passages under the agreed process. This did not make translation free of interpretation. It made the route from a spoken contribution to the exhibition’s written form visible enough that people could ask what had been preserved, condensed or explained.

F

Removing a face did not always make a participant unidentifiable. A distinctive stall, a work uniform or a sequence of locations could reveal who was shown to a local viewer. The team assessed these contextual clues instead of treating a blurred face as a universal privacy switch. Different audiences could recognise different features. A detail obscure to the curators might be obvious to neighbours. Where a person’s participation depended on limited identification, the project checked the whole image and caption against that condition rather than consider the face in isolation.

G

The photographers’ presence affected some scenes. A vendor rearranged goods for a portrait, and customers paused when they noticed a camera. These were not necessarily worthless images, but they did not show the same situation as an unnoticed observation. The project recorded staged or prompted arrangements where relevant. It resisted calling every image spontaneous simply because the people and setting were real. The account of how a picture was made helped viewers understand what kind of encounter they were seeing and what it could support.

H

Participants who spent time on interviews received the project’s stated payment. The team did not treat this as buying unlimited future consent or as proof that every response had become unreliable. Payment acknowledged a particular contribution under agreed terms. Its existence was documented so viewers could understand the arrangement. A person could value the compensation and still disagree with a proposed use. Separating the payment, the interview and the use permission prevented one transaction from being given more authority than the parties had actually agreed.

I

Local participants helped choose images and themes for the display. Their suggestions sometimes conflicted: one wanted work to appear demanding, another wanted the pleasure of meeting customers to remain visible. The curators did not collapse these preferences into one statement of what the community wanted. They attributed perspectives and explained selection decisions. Consultation influenced the exhibition without becoming evidence that everyone had approved every choice. A collaborative process could preserve disagreement as part of the account, rather than require a single voice before any public presentation was possible.

J

Most photographs came from two busy evenings. The team also included an account of the limits of that coverage. A vivid crowd image did not establish that the square was always crowded, and a quiet closing scene did not prove permanent decline. Time, weather and the particular event affected what was visible. The display avoided using one dramatic moment as a complete measure of the market’s economic or social condition. It could describe an observed occasion without claiming that the selected photographs represented every hour, season or kind of visit.

K

Colour adjustments made for printing were recorded. A sequence of pictures could also create a narrative relationship that no single image established. Placing an empty stall after a portrait might suggest an outcome or mood, even if the pictures were taken on different dates. The team checked these implied connections rather than examine each file alone. Editing was part of the exhibition’s argument. It was not automatically deception, but its effects required attention because accurate individual photographs could become misleading when their order invited an unsupported story.

L

Camera timestamps were checked against the event schedule and the photographers’ notes. A device clock could be wrong, and export settings could alter how a stored time was displayed. The team distinguished capture time from upload or editing time. Where exact timing was uncertain, it used a supported date or range instead of preserving false precision. The metadata remained useful evidence when its origin and interpretation were known. It did not gain unquestionable authority simply because the number had been inserted by a machine rather than written by a person.

M

The display plan included a route for later concerns about use. If an image was withdrawn from the project’s own website under the agreement, the team recorded the change and stopped the uses it controlled. It did not promise to erase every copy that another viewer might already have saved. That limitation had to be explained without using it as an excuse to ignore a concern. Managing continuing responsibility meant naming both the available action and the boundaries of control, not announcing either total technical power or complete helplessness.

N

Original files, permission records and interview notes had different access arrangements. The project kept the evidence needed for accountability without placing every private detail in a public folder. A public exhibition could explain its process through selected documentation. It did not require releasing all contact information or every unused conversation. The retention plan named who could inspect sensitive records and for what purpose. Openness about curatorial choices was compatible with limits on disclosure, provided the team did not use privacy as a vague reason to make every decision impossible to examine.

O

The finished exhibition identified itself as a documented encounter with this market under stated conditions. It offered portraits, observations and attributed interpretations rather than claim to contain the whole community. The photographs remained compelling partly because viewers could understand where they came from and what had shaped them. The project’s value did not depend on pretending that permission, representation and editing were settled once the shutter closed. Those relationships continued as the images moved from the square to the wall, the catalogue and the screens on which new audiences found them.

questions.prompt: Collaboration preserved attributed differences rather than present consultation as universal agreement.
questions.explanation: I劳苦与乐趣意见异，署各观点并说明取舍，不说全社区全批准。C组织者权限不是共选之后观点分歧；其他段无该处理。

questions.prompt: Contextual features could identify a person even after their face was obscured.
questions.explanation: F摊位制服地线等本地人认得，糊脸非匿名开关，核全图文字。D caption推收入是断言证据非再识别；其他段无此隐私机制。

questions.prompt: The order of individually accurate photographs was checked for an unsupported implied story.
questions.explanation: K肖像后空摊可暗示结局心境却异日，序列关系须核，非各真即合真。D单图caption不是组照次序，其他段无叙事蒙太奇。

questions.prompt: A caption about feelings and trading success was changed because the image did not establish those claims.
questions.explanation: D照片站摊不证收入产权情绪，删喜悦卖好无据陈述。K图序能暗示但不是该具体caption核实；其他段无这个例。

questions.prompt: Payment acknowledged a contribution without purchasing unlimited control over future uses.
questions.explanation: H报酬为约定访谈时间，非无限同意，也不自动证回答不可信，付酬与许可分。B一般许可未讨论报酬效力；其他段无这项。

questions.prompt: Agreement to be photographed did not automatically extend to every later display or promotional use.
questions.explanation: B同意拍摄与指定展场宣传用途分，持文件不扩许可，按项目约定记。M事后撤图是后续责任非初始授权范围；其他段无这项区分。

questions.prompt: The team responded to later removal concerns within its control without promising to erase every already-saved copy.
questions.explanation: M网站按约撤和停自控用途，承认他人保存副本不可全抹但不借口不理。N记录权限是存档披露非事后撤回控制；其他段无这个边界。

questions.prompt: Two busy evenings did not justify a claim about the market’s condition at every time or season.
questions.explanation: J采两繁忙晚，群照不证总挤，静景不证衰落，记时天气活动。A项目开题非具体覆盖范围；其他段无这两日样本边界。

questions.prompt: An organiser’s help with access was not treated as authority over every person’s participation.
questions.explanation: C组织者助引荐不代表全部商贩访客，后勤与个体同意分。I共选图分歧不是初始代表授权；其他段无组织者权限。

questions.prompt: The making of an image was documented when camera presence or prompting had changed the scene.
questions.explanation: G卖家摆货顾客停，记录摆拍提示，真场真人不必自发。L机器时钟误差不讲摄影者改变行为；其他段无观察影响。

materials.title: One Ticket, Several Meanings
materials.text:
This original fictional case supplies all evidence needed for the questions.

A

A fictional transport district introduced a ticket covering buses and trams. Its publicity promised a simpler journey, but the evaluation team found that one ticket created several different questions. A payment could represent more than one vehicle boarding, an account might represent more than one traveller and a lower fare could leave an inaccessible route unchanged. The new system was examined as a set of travel and payment rules. The report did not assume that integration meant all those rules or all users’ experiences had become identical.

B

A boarding record was not the same as a complete journey. Someone changing from a bus to a tram could create two records while travelling from one origin to one destination. Adding boardings could measure vehicle use, but it would overstate the number of person-journeys if every transfer were counted as a fresh trip. The team named the unit used in each table. It did not abandon boarding totals; it explained what they described and which additional assumptions were needed to connect them into possible journeys.

C

Tickets could be purchased in advance and activated later. The validity period in this system began at activation, not at purchase. A receipt’s sale time therefore did not establish when a passenger started travelling. The interface displayed both stages with clear names. The distinction mattered when a ticket bought the previous day was used in the morning. Staff checked the announced rule rather than assume that every timestamp associated with a ticket represented the same event. A convenient digital record needed an interpretation before it could determine validity.

D

The ordinary transfer window had a stated duration, but a documented disruption could trigger a defined exception under the district’s policy. Staff did not treat this as permission to ignore all limits whenever a passenger was late. The exception specified the relevant disruption and evidence. The evaluation recorded both ordinary and exception-based use so that readers could see how the system operated. A rule could include a transparent response to a failure of service without becoming an unexplained series of personal favours at the discretion of whoever handled a complaint.

E

Daily caps required a definition of the day. The district used a stated service-day boundary that did not coincide with midnight. A late-night passenger could otherwise misunderstand why two boardings fell within the same capped period or why a new period had begun. The team published examples under that local rule and labelled the boundary in the data. The rule was not presented as a universal fact about calendars. It was an administrative choice shaping how the ticket counted expenditure over a named interval.

F

The cap applied through a payment identity. A person using two unrelated cards might split their travel across two records, while a shared account could combine the activity of several people. The analysts therefore did not interpret one account automatically as one unique traveller. The interface explained how the cap accumulated under the chosen payment arrangement. This was a different question from whether a fare was affordable. An apparently simple count of capped users could depend partly on devices and account practices rather than the number of individuals whose journeys had reached a particular cost.

G

Not everyone used the new application. The district retained specified ways to obtain and use tickets without a smartphone and checked whether those channels provided the advertised fare options. A discount shown online was not equally available if another channel could not deliver it. The evaluation separated the existence of a low price from the practical means of accessing it. It also recorded the information given to staff helping passengers. Digital convenience for many users did not by itself establish that all people had a workable route to the same product.

H

Revenue had to be divided among the participating operators. The district chose an allocation formula under its agreement rather than pretend the payment data uniquely revealed a fair split. A transfer journey involved several services, and one integrated price did not itself state what each should receive. The report described the formula and the evidence used in it. This made commercial distribution open to examination without claiming that it was a direct physical measurement like distance. Another agreed formula could answer a different policy objective even with the same underlying travel records.

I

Passenger numbers rose during the pilot, but service frequencies had also changed on some routes. The team considered these concurrent changes before attributing the whole increase to fare integration. A comparison period helped only if relevant differences were described. The report kept the new ticket’s observed use separate from a claim about how many additional journeys it had caused. A popular product could be worth retaining even where the available evaluation did not isolate its independent effect from every timetable and travel-pattern change that occurred around it.

J

Savings varied with travel patterns. Someone making many transfers could benefit differently from a person taking one short ride. A single average concealed that distribution. The team showed examples and grouped results under stated assumptions rather than promise the same saving for every passenger. This did not make a system with unequal savings automatically unfair; a judgement about fairness required an objective and a comparison. The report described who appeared to benefit and where the evidence was limited, leaving the policy choice visible instead of hiding it inside the mean.

K

A passenger survey reached many frequent users at major stops. People who rarely travelled or had stopped using the service were less likely to appear there. The team kept that sampling limitation in the report and used other enquiry routes where possible. A high response total did not make the sample representative by itself. Questions about the ticket could be answered differently by someone who had successfully used it and someone unable to obtain it. The evaluation needed to consider who had an opportunity to contribute, not just how many forms had been returned.

L

A cheaper transfer did not create a bus where none ran at the needed time. The route map and timetable still shaped which journeys were possible. The evaluation considered travel opportunities alongside fare savings rather than treat price as a complete account of access. A resident might face a small charge for an unusable connection or a larger charge for a direct service. The report did not choose one experience as universal. It separated the financial rule from the physical and temporal network in which a passenger had to use it.

M

Travel records could reveal regular locations even when names were removed. Repeated journeys from a small area to the same destination might identify someone to a knowledgeable viewer. Public tables therefore combined information under the district’s access arrangements, while detailed traces remained restricted. The privacy plan concerned patterns as well as explicit identity fields. The team could publish useful findings without release of every individual path. It explained which aggregation had been applied so that a reader understood both the evidence available and the detail deliberately withheld.

N

Fare changes were recorded with their effective dates and the event to which each rule applied. A ticket purchased before a change but activated after it needed a stated treatment. The district preserved the earlier rule rather than overwrite it and make old receipts appear inexplicable. A current price table answered a current sales question; it did not necessarily explain every historical transaction. Keeping rule versions linked to relevant events made later enquiries possible without asking staff to reconstruct the policy from memory or guess which date a system had used.

O

The final evaluation distinguished product use, journey patterns, cost distribution and opportunities to travel. It documented improvements and unresolved questions without forcing them into one unexplained success score. The district could then discuss its aims: simpler payment, fewer transfer penalties, broader access or another priority. Data helped examine consequences under those goals. It could not choose a goal merely by becoming more detailed. The integrated ticket was useful when its users and operators could understand the rules it joined, the differences it preserved and the evidence behind claims made on its behalf.

questions.prompt: The period for a cap used an announced service-day boundary rather than an assumed midnight boundary.
questions.explanation: E封顶日按本地服务日起点，非自然午夜，例和数据均标。D转乘窗口是短时规则非日账边界；其他段无该定义。

questions.prompt: A disruption-based exception was defined and recorded rather than treated as unlimited permission to ignore transfer limits.
questions.explanation: D普通窗口加明确证据条件异常，记录两类，非任迟都免或人情随意。E服务日是账期固定定义，不是中断例外；其他段无这条。

questions.prompt: A transfer could create several vehicle-use records without representing several complete person-journeys.
questions.explanation: B公交转电车两上车可一出行，表须标单位，不能上车数等人程。F账户与个人区别是支付身份，不是车辆登乘与全程；其他段无该计数。

questions.prompt: Reduced prices did not remove timetable and network limits on a person’s possible trips.
questions.explanation: L便宜换乘不生所需时刻无的车，财务与物理时间网络分。G购票途径非实际车辆供给；其他段无此出行机会边界。

questions.prompt: Payment accounts were not automatically interpreted as individual travellers.
questions.explanation: F一人双卡分、共享合多人，达到封顶数受设备账户影响，非唯一人数。B上车数不是账户身份；其他段无此单位界线。

questions.prompt: Historical rule versions were retained to explain transactions spanning a price change.
questions.explanation: N保生效日期和适用事件，购前激后有明确规则，旧价不覆盖。C一般购买激活之别无价格版本历史；其他段无该处理。

questions.prompt: Access to a low fare was checked for people using channels other than a smartphone application.
questions.explanation: G保留无智能机渠道并核能否同票价，存在低价不等人人可得。L无车接驳限制非支付渠道；其他段无购票可达性。

questions.prompt: Anonymised-looking route data could still identify someone through recurring locations.
questions.explanation: M去名仍可由规律起终点认人，公开汇总原轨迹限权。F账户多人是计数归属非重识别，其他段无该模式隐私。

questions.prompt: The start of ticket validity was distinguished from the earlier time at which it was bought.
questions.explanation: C本系统从激活非购买计有效期，界面分时段，前日买次晨用。N价格变更事件归属虽也涉购激时间，但不定义常规有效起点；其他段无此。

questions.prompt: The division of integrated revenue was described as an agreed allocation, not uniquely dictated by the payment itself.
questions.explanation: H多运营分账须约定公式，单价不自说明各份，非自然物理测量。J旅客节省分布不是商户收入分配；其他段无该商业公式。
